Working in Mississippi, Gerry performed pioneering work in microscopical studies of the anatomy of resin-yielding pines, and successfully developed methods to increase yield as well as prolong the working life of trees. She worked toward developing best methods stating, "The microscope reveals many secrets concerning the activities of the tree in producing turpentine and gives these results more quickly than experimental methods alone."[3] Based on her field-based research, Gerry was able to develop a program of "More turpentine, less scar, better pine" that many later attributed as a savior for the struggling industry.

InnovationName: "Mother of the Blues", she bridged earlier vaudeville and the authentic expression of southern blues,
InnovationDescription: Ma Rainey created what is now known as "classic blues" while also portraying black life like never before. As a musical innovator she built on the minstrelsy and vaudeville performative traditions with comedic timing and a hybrid of American blues traditions she encountered in her vast tours across the country. She helped to pioneer a genre that appealed to North and South, rural and urban audiences.[31]  Her signature low and gravelly voice sung with Rainey's gusto and authoritative style inspired imitators from Louis Armstrong, Janis Joplin and Bonnie Raitt among others.[31]  In her lyrics, Rainey portrayed the black female experience like few others of the time reflecting a wide range of emotions and experiences.

InnovationName: Innovator in African-American modern dance
InnovationDescription: Dunham was an innovator in African-American modern dance as well as a leader in the field of dance anthropology, or ethnochoreology. Taking inspiration from African-based dance where one part of the body plays against one another, she focused on articulating the torso in her choreography; this became known as the Dunham Technique. At the height of her career in the 1940s and 1950s, Dunham was renowned throughout Europe and Latin America and was widely popular in the United States. The Washington Post called her "dancer Katherine the Great." For almost 30 years she maintained the Katherine Dunham Dance Company, the only self-supported American black dance troupe at that time. Over her long career, she choreographed more than ninety individual dances. She was a pioneer of Dance Anthropology, established methodologies of ethnochoreology, and her work gives essential historical context to current conversations and practices of decolonization within and outside of the discipline of anthropology.  As part of her Masters thesis did ethnographic studies of dance in Haiti, Jamaica, Martinique & Trinidad.  Developed the Dunham Technique of Dance.

InnovationName: Traditional basketry of the Penobscot tribe of Maine.
InnovationDescription: Theresa Secord (b.1958) is a traditional Penobscot basket maker and the founding director of the Maine Indian Basketmakers Alliance (MIBA). Theresa received the National Heritage Fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts in 2016.  In 2009, she was honored with the First Peoples Fund Community Spirit Award and in 2003, the Prize for Creativity in Rural Life by the Women’s World Summit Foundation, presented at the UN in Geneva, Switzerland; for helping basket makers rise out of poverty. Theresa learned to weave ash and sweet baskets on Indian Island from her mentor, the late Madeline Tomer Shay (Penobscot) beginning in 1988.  She weaves family and tribal styles on antique wooden forms, using tools handed down to her from her great-grandmother, Philomene Saulis Nelson. Theresa has taught more than a dozen apprentices to weave baskets and her own work resides in museum and private collections across the nation. She is currently mentoring her own son again, Caleb Hoffman.

InnovationName: Mental Health Checkin Chart for High School
InnovationDescription: In her high school classroom, Castillo introduced a check-in chart for her students. When using the check-in chart, students are encouraged to grab a post-it, write their name on the back and place it next to the statement that best matches their feelings for the day. The options are, "I'm great," "I'm okay," "I'm meh," "I'm struggling," "I'm having a hard time and wouldn't mind a check-in" or "I'm in a really dark place." The last two statements merit a check-in with Castillo and a follow-up conversation with the counselor or the school psychologist on campus. Castillo feels that mental health should be given the same amount of care and consideration as physical health. Using this chart she wants to educate America’s youth about the dangers of ignoring their mental health. Advocates for checking in with students & paying attention to the whole child before trying to access academics. Has set up an "affirmation station" where students can acknowledge accomplishments of their peers & a "shredding station" where students can shred their negative thoughts.  A free copy of her poster chart is available at:  teacherspayteachers.com/Product/Mental-Health-Check-In-Poster-4435675

InnovationName: Remark Glass

It is a zero-waste certified, woman owned business that creates hand-blown glassware and lighting from recycled bottles. They collect glass from local restaurants and community members in Philadelphia, and transform them into unique and sustainable products. They also have a sister non-profit organization called Bottle Underground (founded 2020), which aims to solve the larger waste issue of glass. They have been featured on Good Morning America, Forbes, and The I on MSN.com. “Alongside our sister non-profit Bottle Underground, every glass purchased is a bottle diverted from the landfill.” They have created a keepsake line that transforms a glass keepsake (usually a bottle) from a special occasion into a home accessory like a bowl, pitcher or lamp

InnovationName: 1899 Street sweeper designed to automate the process of cleaning city streets.
InnovationDescription: The first invention credited to Parpart is a street sweeper designed to automate the process of cleaning city streets. Parpart filed two patents for this invention (No. 649,609[32] in 1899 and no. 762,241 in 1901), both of which listed Hiram D. Layman as co-inventor despite his being only an investor. The sweeper was designed to reduce the manual labor involved in street sweeping by providing an automated mechanism to "efficiently gather dirt from the street-surface regardless of inequalities" and deliver the dirt by an onboard elevator to a storage receptacle that could then discharge it into carts. Also important in the design was that the sweeper would be covered, reducing dirt and dust in the air during its operation. An early electric refrigerator was invented by Florence Parpart in 1914. She holds patents for industrial swe.eping machine & electrical refrigerator

InnovationName: Hug Machine, also call Squeeze Box
InnovationDescription: A hug machine, also known as a hug box, a squeeze machine, or a squeeze box, is a therapeutic device designed to calm hypersensitive persons, usually individuals with autism spectrum disorders. The device was invented by Temple Grandin to administer deep-touch pressure, a type of physical stimulation often self-administered by autistic individuals as a means of self-soothing.[1][2]  Autistic people often have sensory processing disorder, which entails abnormal levels of stimulation of the senses (such as hypersensitivity).[3] Because of difficulty with social interactions, it can be uncomfortable or impractical to turn to other human beings for comfort, including hugs. Grandin addressed this by designing the hug machine, in part to help her own anxiety and sensory sensitivity. age 18 invented a hug box-a device to calm those on the autism spectrum she invented to calm herself; 1986 published her book, Emergence: Labeled Autistic, where she publicly discussed her struggles with autism; her book, Developing Talents, 2nd Edition, explores many unnoticed aspects of vocational rehabilitation programs that provide job training and placement for people with disabilities, as well as Social Security Administration programs that offer vocational assistance; 1995, published "Thinking in Pictures, an autobiography showcased her belief that all autistic people saw the world in picture like she did but the 2nd edition published in 2006 identified 3 types of autism-1. Visual Thinkers like she is, who think in photographically specific images. 2. Music and Math Thinkers – who think in patterns and may be good at mathematics, chess, and programming computers. 3. Verbal Logic Thinkers – who think in word details, and she noted that their favorite subject may be history; 2013 published The Autistic Brain: Thinking Across the Spectrum; 1980 published her first two scientific articles on beef cattle behavior during handling; was one of the first scientists to report animals are sensitive to visual distractions in handling facilities such as shadows, dangling chains, and other environmental details that most people do not notice; developed a center track (double rail) conveyor restrainer system for holding cattle during stunning at large beef slaughtering plants; developed an objective, numerical scoring system for assessing animal welfare at slaughtering plants; has also written about the effect of hair whorl position on cattle behavior, the influence of stress prior to slaughter upon meat quality, religious slaughter, mothering behavior of beef cows, cattle temperament, and causes of bruising; designed curved corrals she adapted with the intention of reducing stress, panic, and injury in animals being led to slaughter; contributing editor to MEAT+POULTRY; consults for firms with McDonald’s, Burger King, and Swift to focus on ethical slaughtering practices;

InnovationName: Research on Pink Fairy Armadillo
InnovationDescription: Superina began studying armadillos in western Argentina 25 years ago. Today, she leads an international team that monitors global populations of anteaters, sloths, and armadillos but, thanks to her pink fairy armadillo obsession, she has also become the leading expert on the diminutive and enigmatic animal.  Studying the animal in its natural habitat, however, has eluded her—and everyone else. For centuries the armadillo has evaded the most determined scientists; even Charles Darwin failed to collect a specimen during his visit to Argentina. The pink fairy remains as mysterious as its name suggests because of its subterranean lifestyle, the result of adaptation to a changing environment millions of years ago.

InnovationName: 2015 lead for Mars helicopter technology at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
InnovationDescription: Since 2015, Aung has been the lead for Mars helicopter technology demonstration. The atmosphere on Mars is only 1% of the atmospheric density on Earth, so a key question was how to generate enough lift for flight. The helicopter had to be very light-weight, and its blades had to be able to spin much faster than they would need to do on Earth. In addition, the helicopter could not be controlled by someone on Earth because radio signals take too long to get to Mars. So engineers at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory equipped Ingenuity with a computerized system that allows it to stabilize itself and navigate on its own.

InnovationName: Finkbeiner Test, checklist to help science journalists avoid gender bias in articles
InnovationDescription: The Finkbeiner test is a checklist proposed by freelance journalist Christie Aschwanden to help journalists avoid gender bias in media articles about women in science. To pass the test, an article about a female scientist must not mention: That she is a woman, her husband's job, her childcare arrangements, how she nurtures her underlings, how she was taken aback by the competitiveness in her field, how she is a role model for other women, how she's the "first woman to ..."

InnovationName: 1998 - Book 'After the death of a child'
InnovationDescription: Refusing to fall back on pop jargon about “recovery” or to offer easy solutions or standardized timelines, Finkbeiner’s is a genuine and moving search to come to terms with loss. Her complex profiles of parents resonate with the honesty and authenticity of uncomfortable emotions expressed and, most importantly, shared with others experiencing a similar loss. Finally, each profile exemplifies the many heroic ways parents learn to live with their pain, and by so doing, honor the lives their children should have lived,  the book was prompted by the death of her son & her own reactions; co-proprietor of a science-ish blog, The Last Word on Nothing; her blog comments on what she wasn't going to write about when writing about women scientists inspired Christie Aschwanden to formalize the items & create The Finkbeiner Test a checklist to help science journalists avoid gender bias in articles about women in science-it asks writers to avoid describing women scientists in terms of stereotypically feminine traits, such as their family arrangements;.

InnovationName: Using IBM systems, supervised the mathematical basis for implosion simulations at Los Alamos

For six months, with the help of an assistant, Livesay designed and implemented plug-board programs, punched cards, and carried cards over from one machine to another. With this training in hand, Livesay arrived at Los Alamos in February 1944. She was assigned to work with a theoretical group calculating the predicted shock wave from an implosion-type bomb. Since this group would be using IBM machines, Livesay was well qualified. Her position involved supervising the crew that kept the IBM machines running 24 hours a day, as well as performing hand calculations to check for any errors made by the machines.

InnovationName: Member of the team which built and experimented with the Chicago Pile-1, nuclear reactor for Manhattan Project
InnovationDescription: At age 23, Woods was a member of the team which built and experimented with the world's first nuclear reactor (then called a pile), Chicago Pile-1, in a project led by her mentor Enrico Fermi. Woods was instrumental in the construction and then utilization of geiger counters for analysis during experimentation. She was the only woman present when the reactor went critical. InnovationName: Identification for acidic volcanoes
InnovationDescription: Bascom contributed to a special type of identification for acidic volcanoes. Her article, "The Structures, Origin, and Nomenclature of Acidic Volcanic Rocks of South Mountain", begins by identifying various rock structures formed by the volcano. Bascom argues that South Mountain's rock formations have changed over time, with some rocks originally showing signs of being rhyolite, but now holocrystalline rock. These rocks defy the nomenclature used to identify rocks invented by German and English scientists, so she created prefixes to add to these pre-existing names, to identify acidic changes in rocks. The prefixes she came up with are meta-, epi-, and apo-. Bascom presented a second notable new conclusion regarding the cycles of erosion within Pennsylvania; earlier scientific thought was that the Piedmont province of Pennsylvania was made by two to three erosion cycles, while she discovered that there were at least nine cycles. Bascom found this by compiling a stratigraphic record of Atlantic deposit in the province, listing the depth, unconformities, and different grain sizes (like sand, clay, or gravel). The cycles occurred over a large period of time, with six cycles occurring in the post-Cretaceous period and three occurring in the Cretaceous period. This conclusion gave scientists new ideas about erosion cycles regarding their rate of occurrence and how to define a cycle. In 1896, Bascom worked as an assistant for the USGS. Her role in the team was to study crystalline schists in a square degree of area along eastern Pennsylvania and Maryland, as well as a portion of northwest Delaware. For part of her life as a teacher, Bascom simultaneously worked in the geological survey and her work lead to a multitude of comprehensive reports of geologic folios.

In the summer she learned flying and obtained her private pilot's license. In 1943 she applied to join the Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASP) program. InnovationName: Railroad - Invention of the Gibbon track
InnovationDescription: The Gibbon track was composed of four main parts: the rail, the chair, the tie-bar, and the wedge.  The rail consisted of a head section and a flange section. The web of both sections, located directly under the center of the bearing surface, was mortised every two and one half feet of the rail to receive the wedge locks. Combined, the two sections created a complete rail; where head sections joined they were supported by solid flange section and where flange sections joined they were supported by solid head section. Through this series of underlapping and overlapping rails, a jointless track that evenly distributed load was formed.

InnovationName: Railroad - Anti-derailment device for trains
InnovationDescription: In 1898, Beasley was awarded a patent for a "Means for preventing derailment of railroad-cars".[19] As higher train speeds were now attainable by the use of electric power, train tracks needed additional safeguards to reduce the possibility of derailment. Beasley's anti-derailment device is a combination of a guardrail and locking device. The guardrail uses a strong top flange (a protruding edge or rim), located at the inner side of the track rail, which engages with a detent (a mechanical catch) connected to the train. In the event of a train car about to derail, the detent and flange prevent the car from leaving the track and restore regular motion. The detent must be rigidly framed in position to avoid the risk of straining and being wrenched from its fastenings.[19]

InnovationName: 1950 - Disposable kidney basin for use in hospital environments
InnovationDescription: * Blount invented a disposable kidney-shaped disposable cardboard dish made out of flour, water, and newspaper that was baked until the material was hard  * The concave shape of the small basin fits into the curves of a human body  * By making it disposable, the danger of passing infections from one patient to another was eliminated * U.S. Veterans Affairs (VA) showed no interest in Blount's invention so she sold the rights to her invention to a company in Belgium.

InnovationName: 1942 First African American officer in the Civil Air Patrol
InnovationDescription: Brown was one of few women who attended Curtiss–Wright Aeronautical University where she studied aircraft maintenance and earned an aircraft mechanic's license in 1935. She earned a private pilot's license in 1938 and a commercial pilot's license in 1939, becoming the first African American woman to earn either type of license in the United States. Together with Cornelius Coffey and Enoch P. Waters, Brown formed the National Negro Airmen Association of America, later renamed to National Airmen's Association of America which was incorporated in 1939. Their primary mission was to attract more interest in aviation, help develop a better understanding in the field of aeronautics, and increase African American participation in both fields. She co-founded with Coffey the School of Aeronautics in Chicago, located at Harlem Airport, with the purpose of training black pilots and teaching aviation mechanics. Nearly 200 students from the school went on to join the Tuskegee Airmen. In 1942, she attained the rank of Lieutenant in Civil Air Patrol Squadron 613-6, becoming the first African American officer in the Civil Air Patrol.

InnovationName: Immunization Advocate & Peace Activist
InnovationDescription: founded Peace Links with other congressional wives in 1982 worked with "mainstream women" in the US, Russia & Europe to educate women about the consequences of nuclear arms race & campaigned for world peace, disbanded after end of Cold War in 2001 however some local chapters still function to promote world peace & understanding;1991 co-founder of Every Child by 2 with Rosalynn Carter & campaigned to have every state require immunizations before a child could attend school; with her husband, worked to implement desegregation in Charleston schools; also advocated for eradication of polio through vaccination; CDC adopted her Arkansas model for immunization as a national model

InnovationName: AI Bias
InnovationDescription: 2016 founded Algorithmic Justice League which challenges bias in decision-making software using art; 2011 worked with trachoma program at Carter Center to develop Android-based assessment system for use in Ethiopia; 2013 worked with computer scientists in Zambia to help students become tech creators; her research discovered facial recognition systems found it difficult to identify dark-skinned women; created Aspire Mirror which lets users see a reflection of themselves based on what inspires them; has created 2 films on bias; is CTO for Techturized, Inc a haircare technology company; is working to uncover bias in voice systems; is on Global Technology Panel convened by the Vice President of the European Commission; founded Code 4 Rights in 2014; founded Jovial Designs in 2007; founded Zamrize 2013

InnovationName: Developed Chicxulub Impact Crater Theory
InnovationDescription: her studies of the cenotes that formed the Chicxulub Impact Crater led to her theory that it triggered the extinction event that resulted in the extinction of 50% of the Earth's species & provided scientific eviodence that asteroid collisions can cause climate change & change the biosphere of a planet; 2017 reported on a possible impact crater near Cali Columbia; founder of the Pan American Space Conference; 1996 her team discovered a chain of impact craters in Chad

InnovationName: Instrumental in calculating thrust-to-weight ratio for engine performance
InnovationDescription: During her time at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Canright calculated thrust from rocket engines and analyzed the data to increase performance. One of JPL's, and Canright's, crowning achievements was the successful use of rockets for bomber aircraft. After the successful development of jet propulsion bombers, JPL shifted its focus to designing a rocket which would reach a higher altitude than a helium-filled balloon. Canright, along with Melba Nead, Virginia Prettyman, and Macie Roberts, were responsible for calculating the potential of rocket propellants. In 1943, after the success of designing and testing of a rocket propellant, Canright became pregnant with her first child. Due to the unavailability of maternity leave in 1943, Canright had to resign.

InnovationName: Outspoken critic of the "track system" in secondary education
InnovationDescription: Haynes was an outspoken critic of the "track system" in the DC school system. InnovationName: Hypothesized the topography of the moon surface for an unmanned Rover
InnovationDescription: In the mid-1960s, Buwalda Riggle was working at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, where they were  designing an unmanned moon rover that would carry out survey work ahead of the first moon landing.  The project was led by scientist Phyllis Buwalda, who had been homeschooled on a ranch in Colorado and had a tough, practical intellect. Her team came to her with a problem. We’ve got absolutely no idea what the surface of the moon is like, they said. Is it going to be sandy? Will there be sharp stones? Will it be hilly? We can’t design a vehicle until we know what it’s like.  Phyllis had a brilliant answer. She said: It’s like the desert in the Southwest. Off you go. People asked her afterwards – how did you know? She said: I didn’t. But if I didn’t take away the uncertainty, my team couldn’t do anything, and there wouldn’t be a moon rover. So I just picked out something that I thought was the best bet. And I ruled out things which my team simply couldn’t build for anyway. see https://www.thehrdirector.com/features/leadership/what-the-surface-of-the-moon-can-teach-us-about-leadership-in-the-covid-era/

InnovationDescription: In 1935 Cochran founded her cosmetic line, Wings to Beauty, marketing products meant for a more active woman who wanted to have adventures but also look polished while doing so. InnovationDescription: With a Bachelor’s degree in art history and a Master’s degree in cultural studies, as well as professional experience in several major cultural institutions including the Walters Art Museum and the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Hillary ensures the Makeup Museum solidifies makeup's rightful place in museums and academia. Above all, she strives for for the Museum to be an agent of change within the cosmetics industry and beyond through analyzing both makeup history and contemporary beauty culture. InnovationDescription: Ceruti is the first woman to specialize in the field of high-altitude archaeology, she was team lead on the expedition which found the Children of Llullaillaco. The team’s sculpture was called “Wenabozho and Dadibaajimad Journey on the River of Souls,” and was a homage to Ojibwe artist Jim Denomie, who died in 2022. The piece illustrates a traditional Ojibwe story of two figures—Wenabozho and his brother Dadibaajimad—on an otherworldly journey. According to Ojibwe tradition, when someone dies, they travel the Milky Way in a canoe to join relatives who have passed before them.

InnovationName: Co-founder of the Grupo Austral, which recognized that urban architecture must holistically look at the needs of the city and its culture
InnovationDescription: After obtaining her degree from the School of Architecture of the University of Buenos Aires Villa became involved with the founding of the Grupo Austral in 1938. This group of architects were particularly noted for bringing the modernist movement to Argentina. They were the first group to recognize that the urbanist movement must holistically look at the needs of the city and its culture, rather than randomly building individual structures. They advocated for green space, parks and streets to be designed for meeting the needs of growth and attempted to bring scientific analysis into city planning. While they viewed cultural development as a key component of architectural identity, they did not believe in preserving historic structures for the sake of history but rather whether analysis proved a structure had adaptability to future societal growth and functionality.

InnovationName: Iconic portrait honoring President Franklin D. Roosevelt and the Four Freedoms
InnovationDescription: In 1943, Burke competed in a national contest to win a commission for the sculpture, created from sketches made during a 45-minute sitting with Roosevelt at the White House. Burke herself "wrote to Roosevelt to request a live sitting, to which the president generously agreed. His wife Eleanor Roosevelt objected to how young Burke chose to present him, but she responded by saying, "This profile is not for today, but for tomorrow and all time. The 3.5-by-2.5-foot plaque was completed in 1944 and unveiled by President Harry S. Truman in September 1945 at the Recorder of Deeds Building in Washington, D.C., where it still hangs today.

She was able to codify the technical details of many of the African dances through the notation system she evolved and was also able to view and to salvage some "still existent gems of dances before they faded into general decadence."[22] She has been unselfish in sharing the knowledge she has gained with others.[1]  The significance of Primus' African research and choreography lies in her presentation of a dance history which embraces ethnic unity, the establishment of an articulate foundation for influencing future practitioners of African dance, the presentation of African dance forms into a disciplined expression, and the enrichment of American theater through the performance of African dance

InnovationDescription: * Yellow Bird Woman Cobell was lead plaintiff in groundbreaking class-action suit challenging the United States' mismanagement of trust funds belonging to more than 500,000 individual Native Americans.  * suit challenged the government to account for fees from resource leases. A $3.4 billion settlement for the trust case to partially compensate individual account holders, buy back fractionated land interests, and restore land to reservations.  * provided for a $60 million scholarship fund for Native Americans and Alaskan Natives, named the Cobell Education Scholarship Fund.  * largest settlement ever in a class action against the federal government.

InnovationName: As an astronaut logged over 4,330 hours in space
InnovationDescription: Coleman was selected by NASA in 1992 to join the NASA Astronaut Corps. In 1995, she was a member of the STS-73 crew on the scientific mission USML-2 with experiments including biotechnology, combustion science, and the physics of fluids. During the flight, she reported to Houston Mission Control that she had spotted an Unidentified flying object (UFO). She also trained for the mission STS-83 to be the backup for Donald A. Thomas; however, as he recovered on time, she did not fly that mission. STS-93 was Coleman's second space flight in 1999. She was mission specialist in charge of deploying the Chandra X-ray Observatory and its Inertial Upper Stage out of the shuttle's cargo bay.

InnovationName: 1995 First female to pilot & command a Space Shuttle
InnovationDescription: After working as a flight instructor and test pilot, Collins was the first woman to pilot the Space Shuttle and the first to command a Space Shuttle mission. She was also the first pilot to fly a Space Shuttle orbiter through a complete 360-degree maneuver.

Grove; wrote "Again We Sail" an account of her 1939 voyage on the SS Lewis Luckenback from New York through the Panama Canal to San Francisco

InnovationName: 1967 Designed 1st home pregnancy test
InnovationDescription: Crane designed the 1st home pregnancy test in 1967. She saw test tubes at her work place in Organon and asked what they were. A scientist informed her they were pregnancy tests sent in by doctors, with patients getting the results in up to 2 weeks. Using a paper clip holder, test tube, mirror, and dropper to create her prototype, she presented the results to Organon executives who originally rejected her idea. By 1972 pregnancy tests were available in a Canadian test market, by 1977 on the US market. Although her name was on the patent she didn't receive recognition for her design until after a New York Times article in 2012 didn't credit her  she wrote to the author and was then credit for this innovation for the 1st time.

InnovationName: Leader in the field of Critical Race Theory
InnovationDescription: a founder of the field of Critical Race theiory; 2011 founder & Director of the Center for Intersectionality & Social Policy Studies at Columbia Law School; 1991 assisted the legal team representing Anita Hill at the US Senate confirmation hearings for Supreme Court Justice Clarence thomas; 1996 co-founder & Executive director of African American Policy Forum (AAPF) a think tank focused on dismantling structural inequality & advancing & expanding racial justice, gender equality, & the indivisibility of all human rights in the US &  internationally; 1989 coined the term "intersectionality" as a way to explain the oppression of African-American women; her work in intersectionality was instrumental in drafting the equality clause in the Constitution of South Africa; with the support of the Rockefeller Foundation facilitates the Bellagio Project an international network of scholars working in the field of social inclusion from 5 continents

InnovationDescription: 1875 patented an upgraded version of the union suit, and dubbed it the “emancipation suit” a gathered section freed the breasts from compression, while sets of buttons at the waist & hips helped suspended several layers of skirts, it could also be purchased as 2 separate pieces which buttoned at the hips; they were called emancipation suits because they emancipated women from the confines of corsets; her suits were the 1st to attract widespread attention but they were still considered ugly

InnovationName: 1964 Nobel Prize, Pioneer in x-ray crystallography & structures of molecules
InnovationDescription: Crowfoot Hodgkin identified & confirmed structures of molecules using x-ray crystallography, the experimental science of determining the atomic and molecular structure of a crystal. By measuring the angles and intensities of the X-ray diffraction, a crystallographer can produce a three-dimensional picture of the density of electrons within the crystal and the positions of the atoms, as well as their chemical bonds, crystallographic disorder, and other information. Using this tool, she was able to map penicillin's 17 atoms in four years. It took her eight years to map the 181 atoms of vitamin B-12, and 34 years for the 788 atoms of insulin; she considered the last to be her crowning achievement. Crowfoot Hodgkin’s work was instrumental in paving the way for the mass-production of insulin, used on a large-scale for the treatment of type 1 & 2 diabetes. Her work with penicillin allowed it to be mass-produced and is widely used as an antibiotic. She was the first to completely determine the structure of a complex organic molecule (cholesterol) by x-ray crystallography. Crowfoot Hodgkin was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964 for her work.
Category: Biology - Molecular Biology, Biochemistry, X-ray crystallography

InnovationName: 2017 Developer of the LightSound device for the visually impaired.
InnovationDescription: Bieryla is one of the developers of the LightSound device, designed and developed in 2017 as a tool for the Blind and Low Vision (BLV) community to experience a solar eclipse with sound. The device uses a technique called sonification which is the process of converting data (or light intensity in this case) to sound. As the Moon eclipses the Sun during a Solar Eclipse the sunlight begins to dim and the LightSound device will output a change in musical tone. The device can be attached to headphones or to a speaker to project the sound for a group. LightSound is powered by either by a 9V battery, rechargeable Li-ion battery, or by connecting it to a laptop via USB. Data can be collected and saved for later analysis or sonification when the device is connected to a computer.

InnovationName: Defended the Everglades from being drained & developed
InnovationDescription: early 1920s wrote "Martin Talbot of North Dakota is Walking Florida Now" a ballad about the death of a 22-year-old vagrant beaten to death ion a labor camp which eventually led to a law banning convict leasing in florida; with her friend Elizabeth Virrick, helped pass a law requiring all homes in Miami to have toilets & bathtubs after learning there was no running water or sewer hook-ups in the racially segregated part of Coconut Grove; 1969 founded Friends of the Everglades to protest the construction of a jetport in the Big Cypress portion of the Everglades; co-founder of the Friends of the Miami-Dade Public Libraries with Helen Muir; engaged in charitable work to improve society such as campaigns against slum lords & to improve housing conditions, free milk for babies whose parents needed aid & ratification of the Women's Suffrage Amendment

InnovationName: Explosives Tech
InnovationDescription: explosives technician who conducted early testing at the Manhattan Project because she had small fingers & could easily reach inside bombs to set triggers; she and her group tested various configurations of the conventional explosives assemblies that would be used to detonate both the Hiroshima and Nagasaki weapons & were the assembly crew for the world's first nuclear explosion, code-named Trinity, which took place at the Alamogordo Bombing Range in a desert area of south-central New Mexico on July 16, 1945;

InnovationName: Creator of Dunyementaries
InnovationDescription: first out black lesbian to ever direct a feature film with her 1996 film The Watermelon Woman, an exploration of the history of black women and lesbians in film; runs the production company Jingletown Films based in Oakland, California; work often concerns themes of race, sexuality, and gender, particularly issues relating to black lesbians; developed "Dunyementaries," a self-coined blend of narrative and documentary techniques that she describes as "a mix of film, video, friends, and a lot of heart." (Wikipedia)

InnovationName: US Army Anti-segregationist
InnovationDescription: founded the Black Leadership Development Program (BLDP) in Dayton Ohio in 1982 to educate & train African-Americans to be leaders in their communities; created Parity or Parity Inc in 2000 to facilitate BLDP's training program; fought against segregation & opened doors for African-American women in the military; while commanding the 6888th she developed a new system of organizing & tracking mail & tracking individual service members by maintaining over 7 million information cards which included serial numbers to distinguish members with the same or similar names; her battalion processed over 195,000 pieces of mail & packages daily to clear the backlog in 3 months; 1945 she & her unit transferred to France to clear another backlog of military mail; she & her unit eventually cleared over 17 million pieces of mail during the war

InnovationName: Military Service

InnovationName: 1832 Established the first racially integrated school in the United States.
InnovationDescription: In 1831 Crandall purchased the Elisha Payne house, with her sister Almira Crandall, to establish the Canterbury Female Boarding School. With the help of her sister and a maid, she taught about forty children in different subjects including geography, history, grammar, arithmetic, reading, and writing. The school flourished until September 1832, when Sarah Harris, the daughter of a free African-American farmer near Canterbury, asked to be accepted to the school to prepare for teaching other African Americans. Although Crandall was uncertain about whether to admit Harris, whom she liked, she consulted her Bible; she then admitted the girl. With this, Crandell establishing the first integrated school in the United States.

InnovationName: Wrote pioneering legislation & created long-lasting political organizations
InnovationDescription: co-founder and co-editor with her brother Max Eastman of the radical arts and politics magazine The Liberator (1918-1922); co-founder of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom, and co-founder in 1920 of the American Civil Liberties Union; 1909 was appointed to the New York State Commission of Employee's Liability and Causes of Industrial Accidents, Unemployment and Lack of Farm Labor &  drafted the inaugural workers' compensation law, a model that became the standard for the U.S.; advocated for "motherhood endowments" whereby mothers of young children would receive monetary benefits; 1913 co-founded  Congressional Union for Woman Suffrage, which became the National Woman's Party; co-wrote the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), first introduced in 1923; delivered the speech, "Now We Can Begin", following the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment, outlining the work that needed to be done in the political and economic spheres to achieve gender equality; organized the First Feminist Congress in 1919; 1909 helped her brother Max establish the Men’s League for Women’s Suffrage; co-founder American Union Against Militarism

InnovationName: Botany
InnovationDescription: credited with building the botanical collection at the California Academy of Sciences (CAS) in San Francisco & is credited with saving the academy's type plant collection after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake retrieving 1,497 specimens from the damaged building; published over 310 scientific articles and authored 395 land plant species names; there are seventeen currently recognized species named for her, as well as the genera Eastwoodia and Aliciella; served as editor of the biological journal Zoe and as an assistant editor for Erythea before the 1906 earthquake, and founded a journal, Leaflets of Western Botany (1932–1966), with John Thomas Howell; wrote and published the first book on flora in central Colorado, A Popular Flora of Denver, Colorado, in 1893; helped found the American Fuchsia Society, the Tamalpais Conservation Club, the San Francisco Botanical Club, the California Botanical Club, the California Horticultural Society, & the California Spring Blossom & Wildflower Association

InnovationName: Led the design, construction & operation of Tevatron
InnovationDescription: led the design, construction & operation of Tevatron at the Fermi National Accelerator Lab & for 25 years it was the most powerful particle collider in the world; 1985 it recorded its 1st proton-antiproton collisions; 1995 it was used to find the top quark; 2000 it was used to find the tau neutrino; 1989 to 1992 was involved in the Superconducting Super Collider in Texas which was subsequently abandoned; after 1992 made significant contributions to the development of high-gradient, superconducting linear accelerators as well as bright and intense electron sources; played a key role in working with scientists at DESY to develop superconducting accelerator technology; led a Fermilab group collaborating with DESY in the 1990s and built the photoinjector for the TESLA Test Facility at the German laboratory; she & her team developed the Rutherford wire, a configuration of 23 strands of wire that had the perfect mechanical form for use in a magnet

InnovationName: Semiconductors
InnovationDescription: worked on military vision systems for missiles used in both Gulf Wars; holds 6 patents

InnovationName: Developed & fabricated the 1st prosthetic mitral valve
InnovationDescription: designed & fabricated the 1st artificial mitral valve prostheses (1959) & led the team that implanted it in a human (1960); developed a cloth covered mechanical valve known as the Braunwald-Cutter Valve; developed the stented aortic hemograft (a graft of human tissue) for mitral valve replacement, surgical treatment of chronic thromboembolic disease, & pioneering techniques for the use of tissue cultures to discourage the formation of clots when prosthetic valves & circulatory assist devices are used; helped design a cardiopulmonary bypass machine; developed a pediatric cardiopulmonary bypass pump

InnovationDescription: * Erukhimova uses Tik Tok as a platform to teach physics experiments & make them fun * Uses a range of everyday objects in her experiments, from ping-pong balls and toilet paper to marshmallows, bicycle wheels and hair dryers * On faculty at Texas A & M as Chair for Physics Outreach * Awarded for developing and disseminating innovative physics education programs for college students and the public *Her experiments have radically increased the following of Texas A & M Physics & Astronomy's social media accounts * Her favorite audience to teach is 2nd graders.

InnovationName: Paleontology
InnovationDescription: founded the University of California Museum of Paleontology (UCMP) and the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology (MVZ); after the death of her father in 1904 she dedicated her life to preserving the wild flora and fauna of California and the West Coast; through an anonymous donation, established in 1920 the Folklore Foundation at Vassar College; funded & went on numerous fossil collecting expeditions & amassed a large collection of fossils & exotic game animals she later donated to the museums she founded

InnovationName: Cognitive Science
InnovationDescription: a world leader in a number of fields – child development, language acquisition, aphasia research, cross-linguistic research, bilingualism, psycholinguistics and their neural underpinnings, and had trained, supported and collaborated with a diverse and international group of researchers and students. With Brian MacWhinney, Bates developed a model of language processing called the competition model, which views language acquisition as an emergentist phenomenon that results from competition between lexical items, phonological forms, and syntactic patterns, accounting for language processing on the synchronic, ontogenetic, and phylogenetic time scales.[6] She was a main proponent of the functionalist view of grammar, in that communication is the main force that drives language's natural forms.[7] This view provides support for Bates’ widely known perspective: the brain does not use specialized linguistic centers, but instead employs general cognitive abilities in order to solve a communicative conundrum.[8] Much of her research provided evidence towards the core principles of empiricism and against the nativist school of thought, which made her a major player in the East Pole-West Pole divide of cognitive psychology and cognitive neuroscience.  She highlighted the reliance on pointing by infants in order to fill their need to communicate before they are able to speak.[9] The child's ability to incorporate imperatives in their gestures in order to make a command or request was found in her research and shows the necessity of communication regardless of language.[10] Bates also coined the term protoword, a word-like utterance made by prelinguistic children that has meaning (e.g. yumyum), but does not represent the adult-like form. She found that regardless of the strategy applied by the child, they learn words at the same rate.[12] She did, however, find strong predictive power in the child's vocabulary at 13 and 20 months old and their grammatical complexity at 2 years old.[13] Bates finds that language learning comes from the neural plasticity in the brain; therefore, children can and are able to learn a language, even with brain trauma. showed that after brain injury, adult aphasic patients' deficits were not specific to linguistic structures theorized to be localized to specific brain areas,[15] or even restricted to the linguistic domain. She demonstrated that neural plasticity allows children with damage to the right hemisphere or the left hemisphere to learn and use language within normal range.

InnovationName: First woman to execute modern-style code on a computer
InnovationDescription: first woman to execute modern-style code on a computer; made significant contributions to the world of programming, including work on the Monte Carlo method (a method to store and analyze large quantities of data and make predictions on everything from elections to COVID-19 trend forecasting), ENIAC, and MANIAC; programmed the MANIAC I machine, which could store data, designed by her husband and Julian Bigelow; worked on the ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) on a project with her husband to produce the first successful meteorological forecast on a computer; designed new controls for ENIAC;

InnovationName: Co-founder The Seeing Eye a dog guide school
InnovationDescription: co- founded The Seeing Eye, with Morris Frank, the first dog guide school for the blind in the United States in Nashville TN in 1929; credited with helping to change public attitudes toward the disabled and contributing to the disability rights movement that began in the 1970s; she & 1st husband Walter Wood established an experimental farm for breeding dairy cattle to improve milk production in Hoosick Falls NY with the help of the US Dept of Agriculture in 1906 & continued to run it for 2 years after his death in 1915; 1929-33 was President of L'Oeil Qui Voit a Swiss training school for dogs & instructors

InnovationName: Work in fluid dynamics, specifically in the areas of aircraft turbulence and spiraling airflows.
InnovationDescription: Widnall is internationally known for her work in fluid dynamics, specifically in the areas of aircraft turbulence and spiraling airflows. She designed MIT's advanced wind tunnel facility. One of her most notable works is on the elliptical instability mechanism with Raymond Pierrehumbert. She published research that analyzed vortices trailing from the wing tips of aircraft that was used to gauge the hazards of wake turbulence, known as the Widnall instability. She was the first director of the office of university research at MIT for the U.S. Department of Transportation. While she was Secretary of the Air Force she began the program to develop the expendable launch vehicle used for Atlas 5 and Delta 4 rockets. She was Co-Chair of the 2018 NAS/NAE/NIM report on the Sexual Harassment of Women in Science and Technology.
Invention: Wingsail with adaptable flexible flap; Flexible tailored elastic airfoil section; Fiber velocity imparter device for dry-forming systems

InnovationName: Author of The Fannie Farmer Cookbook
InnovationDescription: insisted on exact, precise measurements in her recipes thus standardizing measurements in cooking for the 1st time in the USA; transformed cooking & recipes into a science; established the convention that ingredients for a recipe would be given in the order required

InnovationName: Study of Human Movement
InnovationDescription: studied the role of gender in the culture of science; work focused on the interrelations of environment, technology, and economics, and on weighing the environmental risks and costs of technological growth against the benefits to society; as Associate Director of Continuum Movement Arts taught Continuum; created PHYSIKOS (ran it 2006-2013), a studio dedicated to contemplative and somatic movement art; co-author of "A Moving Inquiry: The Art of Personal Practice" with Beth Pettengill Riley in 2019, a guide to establishing a personal movement practice that can serve as the foundation of daily life, with the body itself as teacher;

InnovationName: 1984 First female dean of an engineering school in the USA
InnovationDescription: In 1984 Baum was named dean of Pratt Institute's School of Engineering in New York, a distinctive role because it made her the first woman dean of an engineering school in the United States. Three years later, she became dean of the Albert Nerken School of Engineering at Cooper Union, and is now dean emeritus.

InnovationName: Creating aquafarming business in Maine
InnovationDescription: marine ecologist at the University of Maine known for her research on algae especially algal reproduction & the promotion of growing algae as a food source; Editor of the Journal of Phycology from 1996 until 2001; has modeled fertilization and the physical transport of gametes from algae; has tracked the movement of invasive species including periwinkles and the toothed wrack seaweed, Fucus serratus, where her research revealed that both originated from Ireland and Scotland and were likely carried in ballast rocks on ships that were moving materials across the Atlantic Ocean; her research on electrical currents measured during the development of wild carrot, a flowering plant, revealed that the chemical indole-3-acetic acid rapidly stopped the current in the plant's cells; led the team examining the genome of the red algae Porphyra and the resulting research revealed how they survive by transporting nutrients, protecting themselves from light, and form cell walls; her research has implications for aquaculture and the new marketing of sea vegetables, including Ascophyllum, as a new cash crop in Maine; was a key member of Maine’s Department of Marine Resources’ Rockweed Fishery Management Project Development Team in 2013;

InnovationName: Ecology
InnovationDescription: Founder of The Endocrine Disruption Exchange (TEDX 2003) a research organization devoted to understanding how environmental exposures to endocrine disruptors interfere with development and health; an environmental health analyst, and best known for her studies on the health effects of endocrine disrupting chemicals; Professor Emerita of Zoology University of Florida; established and directed the Wildlife and Contaminants Program at World Wildlife Fund, US;1991, as a fellow of the W. Alton Jones Foundation, she brought a group of 21 scientists with diverse backgrounds together, to attend the first of a series of conferences at Racine, Wisconsin, that became known simply as "Wingspread", about the effects of human exposure to hormone-disrupting chemicals examined in the environment; published and lectured extensively on the consequences of prenatal exposure to synthetic chemicals by the developing embryo and fetus in wildlife, laboratory animals, and humans; contributed to a two-year study of the Great Lakes drainage basin; 1991, published a study about the reproductive challenges faced by bald eagles living in the Great Lakes region; with developmental biologist Frederick S. vom Saal and cell biologist Ana M. Soto coined the term endocrine disruptor in a paper "Developmental effects of endocrine-disrupting chemicals in wildlife and humans," published in 1993; 1996 coauthored a book with environmental journalist Dianne Dumanoski and environmental health scientist John Peterson Myers titled "Our Stolen Future: Are We Threatening Our Fertility, Intelligence, and Survival? A Scientific Detective Story" which spurred the US Congress to pass two acts that led to the creation of the Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program, a program led by the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington D.C. to test new chemicals for their possible effects on endocrine systems

InnovationName: Software Quality Engineering
InnovationDescription: Over twenty years experience in software design verification and validation of medical devices; proven experience in designing project test strategies, leading integration test efforts, coordinating project plans across disciplines, maintaining project related data, and analyzing test results for future enhancements

InnovationName: Environmental Engineering
InnovationDescription: headed a major environmental cleanup at the Chevron El Segundo plant; 1996 was Director of Corporate Liaison at the US Dept of Education; at Chevron, she worked on a project to replace underground tanks to prevent leakage of harmful chemicals throughout Northern California, Idaho and Utah; in Southern California, led a multi-million effort to remove hydrocarbons from the groundwater at the one of the largest refineries; worked to reduce emissions of harmful air pollutants; is skilled at leading transformative efforts, paradigm shifts, and innovative strategies; expertise is engaging stakeholders, policy-makers and government officials, in support of a mission; founding team member of Global Water Farm, Inc (2015-2017) an early-stage, privately-held company whose mission is to cultivate water independence while maintaining and restoring environmental health, vitality and resilience;

InnovationName: Semiconductors
InnovationDescription: made foundational contributions to many emerging areas of science, including the electrical properties of semiconductors, light propagation in optical fibers, and charge motion in quasi-one-dimensional materials; with victor Weisskopf developed the Conwell–Weisskopf formula, which helped underpin the development of the transistor and other semiconductor devices; with William Shockley helped to develop the theory of hot electron transport in germanium; her monograph on high-field transport was influential in the development of semiconductor electronics; made important early contributions on wave propagation in optical fibers; played a crucial role in the emerging field of organic electronic materials and published seminal papers on the theory of the mobility and optical properties of polaronic charge carriers in conjugated polymers and organic semiconductors; Her research was an important part of a substantial effort at Xerox to develop flexible-belt photoreceptors, which became the basis for a highly successful series of products in the 1980s and 1990s;

InnovationName: Designed the equipment and manufacturing processes used to fabricate the ceramic tiles used in the Space Shuttle thermal protection system
InnovationDescription: Dunbar designed the equipment and manufacturing processes to fabricate the ceramic tiles used in the Space Shuttle thermal protection system. In 1978, she joined NASA as a flight controller / payload officer, and was a guidance and navigation controller for Skylab during its de-orbiting and re-entry in July 1979. She was selected as one of the nineteen astronaut candidates in NASA Astronaut Group 9 in 1980. Dunbar flew on five Space Shuttle missions between 1985 and 1998, including two dockings with the Mir space station. She was the principal investigator of the Microgravity Disturbance Experiment using the Fluids Experiment Apparatus.

InnovationName: Work on the Abort-Guidance System
InnovationDescription: Cohen’s work on the Abort-Guidance System is credited with helping save Apollo 13. In other positions she worked as an electrical engineer on the Minuteman missile, the science ground station for the Hubble Space Telescope, the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite, and the Apollo Space Program.

InnovationName: Geological and Tectonic Mapping of Alaska.
InnovationDescription: Dusel-Bacon’s studies have involved deciphering the geologic and tectonic history of east-central Alaska utilizing geologic mapping, metamorphic petrology, whole-rock geochemistry, trace-element tectonic fingerprinting of (meta)igneous rocks, and geochronology (U-Pb zircon,40Ar-39Ar, and apatite fission track data) generated by collaborating scientists. Her studies also have included correlation of regional events in east-central Alaska with those in the western Canadian Cordillera; the age, character, and tectonic setting of submarine, syngenetic, hydrothermal mineral deposits (both volcanic- and sedimentary-hosted); and compilation of a Metamorphic Facies Map of Alaska. Cynthia Dusel-Bacon joined the USGS Branch of Alaskan Geology, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, in 1975. In 1977, during her third field season of geologic mapping in east-central Alaska, she was mauled by a black bear and lost both arms as a result of her injuries. Her disability has not kept her from enjoying a long and productive career that includes fieldwork in Alaska, petrologic studies, and publication of results.

InnovationName: Vaccine Evaluation
InnovationDescription: internationally recognized for her countless contributions to vaccine evaluation and implementation, public health advocacy, and the mentorship and training of new generations of experts in infectious disease over the past four decades; has tested vaccines for H1N1 flu, H5 avian flu, pertussis, pneumococcus, smallpox, anthrax and others; initial studies focused on Haemophilus influenza Type b (Hib) vaccines, where she compared the safety and immunogenicity of four different Hib vaccines in large community pediatric practices and made important contributions to the licensing and universal recommendations for the Hib vaccine; was a founding investigator of the CDC-funded New Vaccine Surveillance Network, assessing the impact of vaccines on respiratory and diarrheal diseases in the United States; her group’s demonstration of the safety and effectiveness of both live and inactivated influenza vaccines in adults and children helped lead to recommendations that all children under 2 years of age should be immunized against flu each year;

InnovationName: 2008 – Management of first Knowledge Management program at Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

InnovationName: 2003 Research into mechanisms of germ cell formation.
InnovationDescription: Extavour conducted a study at Cambridge University on the mechanisms of germ cell formation that showed animal germ cells were likely specified by inductive signals more often than previously thought. This went against the mainstream scientific view that animal germ cells are usually specified by maternally inherited determinants. During a 2013 interview with Quanta Magazine, she explained the concepts of this research as such: "Before there is even an embryo, the molecular content of some cells predetermines them to develop as either germ or soma. In other organisms, there is instead a signaling mechanism: An embryonic cell receives chemical signals from neighboring cells that activate (or repress) the genes that allow for germ-line function."

InnovationName: Development of the theory of Gender Continuum
InnovationDescription: In her writings, Fausto-Sterling has elaborated on the theory of gender continuum, in which gender is not “binary,” or limited to the specific genders “man” and “woman” (or “boy” and “girl”). Instead it is continuous, forming a spectrum of differing degrees and combinations of the mental, emotional, behavioral, and biological traits commonly possessed by or attributed to members of the male or female sex. She has written two books intended for a general audience. The first of those books, Myths of Gender, was first published in 1985. Her second book for the general public is Sexing the Body: Gender Politics and the Construction of Sexuality, published in 2000. In the book she sets out to "convince readers of the need for theories that allow for a good deal of human variation and that integrate the analytical powers of the biological and the social into the systematic analysis of human development."

InnovationName: Engineering
InnovationDescription: Youngest (15 y.o.) African-American female accepted into an Ivy League School; youngest African-American Engineer in the US; speaks 7 languages (English, Spanish, French, Japanese, Russian, Arabic, & German); at 17 youngest IT leader to travel to Cameroon with associate Penn students with "One Laptop Per Child"

InnovationName: Use of wax worms in the breakdown of plastics.
InnovationDescription: Bertocchini’s research focuses on insects, especially wax worms, as biological means to degrade sturdy fossil fuels-derived polymers, i.e. plastics. Her research revealed that the saliva of Galleria mellonella larvae (wax worms) is capable of oxidizing and depolymerizing polyethylene (PE) through the use of 2 enzymes ( Ceres and Demeter). Her research suggests that water-based enzyme solutions could be implemented by waste processing plants or at-home plastic waste kits to break down polyolefin-derived plastics, establishing a wider distribution of this game-changing technology. The end products would only be natural components, such as ketones or alcohol, deemed safe for release or reuse in other processes.

InnovationName: 1797 Wrote  "A Compendious System of Astronomy," a textbook for young girls.
InnovationDescription: Bryan wrote several well-regarded textbooks on astronomy and physics for young women; her first work published in 1797 was, "A Compendious System of Astronomy," a textbook for young girls. Her other works included the physics textbook "Lectures on Natural Philosophy," published in 1806 (thirteen lectures on hydrostatics, optics, pneumatics, and acoustics). A smaller volume, "Astronomical and Geographical Class Book for Schools," was published in 1815 and described the mechanics of the air rifle, the hot air balloon, the diving bell, as well as works of Isaac Newton, Galileo, and Benjamin Franklin, including the latter's experiments with lightning. Bryan created a revised edition of an educational board game, "Science in Sport or The Pleasures of Astronomy," in 1804.

InnovationName: Environmentalist
InnovationDescription: helped establish the Maryland Coastal Bays Program & member of the Assateague Coastal Trust; fought to protect wildlife & against air & water pollution; founded the Worcester Environmental Trust with her husband Joseph W. Fehrer; she and her husband worked on various other environmental projects, including starting the process of creating a water-monitoring program; prevented the building of a harmful dam on Nassawango Creek in the 1980s, and protected the surrounding forest which spanned 10,000 acres; actively fought against offshore waste incarceration and worked to provide her community with clean water; founded The Maryland Coastal Bays Program; co-founder, with her husband, of the Worcester Environmental Trust; with her husband, Joe, canoed the Pocomoke, inventorying the river's environmental and wildlife assets; in the 1980s spearheaded the effort to establish a water quality-monitoring program, prevented the damming of Nassawango Creek and convinced the Nature Conservancy to preserve the creek and upland forest that has grown to 10,000 acres and founded the Nassawango Creek Stewardship Committee that oversees the protection of this area;

InnovationName: Palynology

InnovationName: 1650 first collection of poetry, The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America, was widely read in America and England.

InnovationName: 1970 Early advocate for vermicomposting

Aquaponics combines aquaculture (raising fish) with hydroponics (growing plants without soil). It’s a sustainable system where fish waste provides nutrients for plants, and the plants filter the water for the fish. This offers a closed-loop system for food production during longer space missions.
